title: Perimeter 36, Three Different Sides: How Many Triangles? | AMC 8-Style Level 5

scenes.visual: A loop of string labeled '36' morphing between a few different triangle shapes (e.g. 10-12-14, 5-15-16, 11-12-13), each with side labels. Line 3: one flat 'triangle' 9-9-18 collapses into a line with a red ✗. Line 4: Vantee title card.
lines: Take a string thirty-six units long, and bend it into a triangle.
How many different shapes can you make?
Watch out: some tries go flat, and some repeat a side!
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's count them without missing any.

scenes.visual: Question text left. Line 2: chips 'whole-number sides', 'perimeter 36'. Line 3: chip 'all three sides different'. Line 4: choice chips 17, 19, 20, 27, 35.
lines: Here's the question.
How many triangles have whole-number side lengths and a perimeter of thirty-six,
and have three different side lengths?
Here are the five choices.

scenes.visual: Line 1: example triangle 10, 12, 14 with '10 + 12 + 14 = 36 ✓'. Line 2: example 12, 12, 12 crossed ('sides repeat'). Line 3: tag 'same three sides in a different order = same triangle'.
lines: The three sides must add to thirty-six. For example, ten, twelve and fourteen.
All three must be different, so twelve, twelve, twelve doesn't count.
And the same three sides in a different order make the same triangle. We count it once.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; question visible.
lines: Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.chapter: Solution 1: list by the longest side
scenes.visual: Line 1: tag 'list them, smallest < middle < longest'. Line 2: rule card 'the two shorter sides must add to MORE than the longest'; a demo of 9, 9, 18 lying flat. Line 3: row 'shorter two = 36 − longest > longest' → 'longest < 18'. Line 4: row 'longest ≥ 36 ÷ 3 = 12'. Line 5: range bar 'longest: 12 to 17'.
lines: Welcome back! Let's make an organized list. Write each triangle smallest side first.
Here's the triangle rule. The two shorter sides must add to MORE than the longest side.
The shorter two make thirty-six minus the longest. So the longest side must be less than eighteen.
And the longest side is at least a third of thirty-six. That's twelve.
So the longest side is somewhere from twelve to seventeen.

scenes.visual: A table with one row per longest side, triangles listed as chips 'a, b, c'. Line 1: row 'longest 17: other two add to 19'. Line 2: chips 3,16 · 4,15 · … · 9,10 → count '7'. Line 3: note 'middle < 17, smallest < middle'. Line 4: row 16 (add to 20): 5,15 … 9,11. Line 5: count '5'. Line 6: row 15 (21): 7,14 · 8,13 · 9,12 · 10,11 → '4'. Line 7: row 14 (22): 9,13 · 10,12 → '2'; row 13 (23): 11,12 → '1'. Line 8: row 12 (24): empty → '0', note '10 + 11 = 21 < 24'. Line 9: sum '7 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 19' answer badge, chime at end, choice B highlighted.
lines: Longest side seventeen: the other two add to nineteen.
From three and sixteen up to nine and ten. That's seven.
The middle side has to stay below seventeen, and the smallest below the middle.
Longest side sixteen: the other two add to twenty. From five and fifteen up to nine and eleven.
That's five more.
Longest fifteen: seven and fourteen, up to ten and eleven. That's four.
Longest fourteen gives two. Longest thirteen gives just one: eleven, twelve, thirteen.
Longest twelve gives none. Two different sides below twelve add to at most twenty-one.
Seven plus five plus four plus two plus one is nineteen. That's Choice B!

scenes.visual: Line 1: tag 'all triangles − ones with a repeat'. Line 2: counts by longest side for ALL triangles: '8 + 7 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 27'. Line 3: isosceles triangle drawing with two sides 'x'. Line 4: third side '36 − 2x'. Line 5: row '36 − 2x > 0 → x < 18'. Line 6: row 'x + x > 36 − 2x → 4x > 36 → x > 9'. Line 7: chips x = 10, 11, …, 17 → '8 triangles'. Line 8: chip 12 highlighted '12, 12, 12: equilateral, once'. Line 9: '27 − 8 = 19'. Line 10: small text 'count the leftovers'.
lines: Here's another way. Count every triangle, then take away the ones with a repeated side.
Allow repeats, and the same list grows to twenty-seven triangles in all.
A triangle with a repeat has two equal sides. Call each one x.
So the third side is thirty-six minus two x.
The third side must be more than zero, so x is less than eighteen.
And x plus x must beat the third side, so x is more than nine.
That's x from ten to seventeen: eight triangles.
Twelve, twelve, twelve is one of them, counted just once.
Twenty-seven minus eight is nineteen. Same answer!
When would you pick this way? When the leftovers are easier to count than what you want.

scenes.visual: Choice chips row; each turns red with a short note. Line 1: chip D '27 = all triangles'. Lines 2–3: chip C '27 − 7 = 20', with 12,12,12 circled 'forgot this one'. Line 4: chip E '35 > 27'. Lines 5–6: chip A '17 = 19 − 2', the 'longest 14' row crossed. Line 7: chip B '19' green.
lines: Now the traps. Choice D, twenty-seven, counts every triangle. It forgets to remove the repeats.
Choice C, twenty, removes the repeats but forgets twelve, twelve, twelve.
That's twenty-seven minus seven.
Choice E, thirty-five, is too many. There are only twenty-seven triangles in all!
Choice A, seventeen, is what you'd get if you skipped a row of the list.
For example, the two with longest side fourteen.
An organized list by longest side keeps every triangle, so we land on nineteen.

scenes.visual: Card: 'whole-number sides, perimeter 24, three different side lengths: how many triangles?'.
lines: Ready for a challenge? Now the perimeter is twenty-four.
How many triangles with whole-number sides and three different side lengths are there?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant text visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line: 'longest < 12 and ≥ 8'; row 11 'other two add to 13'; chips 3,10 · 4,9 · 5,8 · 6,7 → '4'; row 10 (14): 5,9 · 6,8 → '2'; row 9 (15): 7,8 → '1'; row 8: '0'; answer badge '4 + 2 + 1 = 7' chime at end of that line; check '12 − 5 = 7'.
lines: Let's check. The longest side must be less than twelve, and at least eight.
Longest eleven: the other two add to thirteen.
Three and ten, four and nine, five and eight, six and seven. Four!
Longest ten: five and nine, six and eight. That's two.
Longest nine: just seven and eight. And longest eight gives none.
Four plus two plus one is seven triangles!
Check another way: twelve triangles in all, minus five with a repeat. Seven!
If you got seven, terrific work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: 'longest side: between a third and a half of the perimeter', 'list row by row', 'or: all − repeats'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Fix the longest side. It's at least a third of the perimeter, and less than half.
Then list row by row. Or count them all, and subtract the repeats.
I'm Vantee. Keep counting, and I'll see you next time!
